content.content:
1	# MonoDreams — Core Tenets
2	
3	> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
4	> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
5	> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
6	> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.
7	
8	## 1. Framework, not library
9	
10	MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
11	the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
12	the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
13	embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
14	low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
15	(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).
16	
17	**Two users, equal weight.**
18	- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
19	  play primitives.
20	- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
21	  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
22	  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.
23	
24	**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
25	general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
26	than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
27	hiding inside the framework.
28	
29	## 2. ECS purity & composition
30	
31	The architecture is composition all the way down:
32	
33	- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
34	  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
35	  logic belongs in a system.
36	- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
37	  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
38	  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
39	  run after.
40	- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
41	  their own.
42	- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
43	  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
44	  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
45	  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
46	  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.
47	
48	**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
49	more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
50	are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
51	should always have more systems than components.
52	
53	**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
54	search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
55	creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
56	this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
57	of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
58	reusable.
59	
60	**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
61	systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
62	Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
63	dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
64	name alone.
65	
66	**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
67	system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
68	just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
69	generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
70	isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.
71	
72	### Aspirational direction
73	
74	- **Declarative system dependencies.** Today, ordering is implicit in
75	  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
76	  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
77	  enforce or warn at registration time.
78	- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
79	  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
80	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
81	  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
82	  closest prototype.
83	- **Test or example per public contract.** New messages, components, and
84	  systems should ship with at least one usage that proves the contract
85	  works and signals that it's maintained.
86	
87	## 3. Hierarchy & Transform
88	
89	`Transform` is the engine's spatial component today. It holds position,
90	rotation, scale, origin, and an optional parent link; it caches a world
91	matrix and exposes `WorldPosition` / `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`
92	properties that walk the parent chain.
93	
94	**Key invariant — don't mix two Transform-shaped components in one
95	project.** A developer is free to write a `MyTransform` with different
96	trade-offs; what breaks the framework is **mixing** `Transform` and
97	`MyTransform` in the same world. Systems should be agnostic enough to
98	operate on either one (see §2 — systems are functions), but the bundled
99	collision, rendering, camera, and culling systems read `Transform`
100	specifically. Using a custom transform means re-implementing those
101	consumers too.
102	
103	**Two parent links, intentionally.** `Transform.Parent` is the matrix
104	link (it determines how `WorldMatrix` cascades); `ChildOf` is a
105	structural marker (it determines lifecycle and cascading disposal). The
106	split exists to support complex hierarchical UI such as a dialogue
107	panel — a single visual whose banner, avatars, text and waiting-indicator
108	move and dispose together but may not all share matrix scaling.
109	`HierarchySystem` keeps the two in sync. **This split is on the refactor
110	backlog** (§10); read both fields when reasoning about hierarchy until it
111	is consolidated.
112	
113	**Dirty propagation.** Mutating a parent's transform marks the entire
114	descendant chain dirty; `WorldMatrix` is a cached property whose getter
115	re-walks the chain when needed. Systems that read `WorldPosition` get
116	the parent-corrected value, but only if `HierarchySystem` has run in the
117	pipeline ahead of them — that's the pipeline assembler's job to arrange.
118	
119	**`Transform.Delta` and `HasMoved`.** These reflect the change between
120	two committed positions. They are meaningful only after
121	`TransformCommitSystem` has run for the *previous* frame. Today no API
122	prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; this is on the backlog as
123	"`Transform` should expose interaction methods that guarantee `Delta`
124	consistency" (§10). For now, downstream systems that depend on `Delta`
125	(notably the collision detection's swept tests) must trust the
126	assembler put `TransformCommitSystem` at the end of every frame.
127	
128	### Aspirational direction
129	
130	Collision, rendering, culling, and camera all read `Transform`
131	directly. The intended end-state is loose coupling — those modules
132	operate against any *Transform-shaped contract*, so a developer can
133	swap in `MyTransform` without re-implementing them. The framework
134	currently doesn't enforce this; treat any `MonoDreams/System/`
135	reference to `Transform` as implementation debt rather than design.
136	
137	## 4. Rendering pipeline
138	
139	The rendering pipeline is the most delicate part of the engine. Bugs
140	here are visual rather than logical, which makes them harder to debug
141	than crashes. Two rules cover most of the surface:
142	
143	**Key invariant — `DrawComponent` is the unified render component.**
144	There is one `DrawComponent` per renderable entity. Its `Type` field is
145	one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, mutually exclusive.
146	Source data lives in companion structs (`SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`,
147	`NinePatchInfo`, mesh buffers) populated by prep systems
148	(`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, `MeshPrepSystem`).
149	**Do not create new draw/render components.** Adding a new visual type
150	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork
151	the pipeline.
152	
153	**Key invariant — `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer.** No game
154	code should call `SpriteBatch` outside the prep-then-master path. A
155	parallel render system is a framework violation — flagged by review.
156	
157	**Key rule — rendering systems run last.** In any pipeline assembly,
158	the prep-cull-sort-render module goes at the end. The recommended order
159	inside the module, from the reference assembly
160	(`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331`), is:
161	`CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` → `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem`
162	→ `MeshPrepSystem` → `MasterRenderSystem`.
163	
164	**Render targets.** Three are defined by `RenderTargetID`:
165	- **Main** — world-space, camera transform applied, **respects culling**.
166	- **UI** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
167	- **HUD** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
168	
169	The `Visible` tag is added and removed by `CullingSystem` based on the
170	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. Only the Main target consults it. UI and
171	HUD entities don't need `Visible`; if you put a `Visible`-gated entity
172	on UI by mistake, it will always render (which is usually the desired
173	outcome anyway — but the failure mode is the reverse: a Main-target
174	entity that never gets `Visible` because no `CullingSystem` is in the
175	pipeline, and the dev stares at an invisible sprite). The renderable
176	entity stack is therefore `EntityInfo + Transform + SpriteInfo +
177	DrawComponent + Visible` for Main, minus `Visible` for UI/HUD.
178	**This split is a known wart** (§10): `Visible` may become a property of
179	`DrawComponent` to remove the easy-to-miss tag.
180	
181	**Layer depth ownership.** Three systems write `LayerDepth` — four when a
182	screen composes scene layers — in this order: `SpritePrepSystem`
183	initializes it from the sprite's layer, the optional `SceneLayerSystem`
184	remaps each scene-layer member's depth from (layer order, within-layer
185	key) while entities on no layer pass through untouched (see §6),
186	`YSortSystem` may override it for entities on Y-sorted layers, and
187	`MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final value. `YSortSystem` uses a
188	minimal epsilon to bias parent-child groups so children stay attached
189	to their parent's depth band. Same-layer entities with the same world Y
190	fall through to insertion order — no other tiebreaker exists; if
191	flicker becomes a problem, that's where to look.
192	
193	**Two coordinate spaces (opt-in).** `ViewportManager` owns an **authoring
194	(layout)** resolution — where every game number is written: entity and UI
195	coordinates, HUD/overlay boxes, camera zoom, culling extents, and the point
196	`MapMouse` returns — and a **render (virtual)** resolution: the pixel size of the
197	render targets and back buffer. They default to being EQUAL, and a game opts in
198	by giving the manager a different layout size. The ratio (`RenderScale`) is
199	applied in **exactly one place — the per-pass render cameras**: world passes take
200	`ViewportManager.CreateCamera()`, screen-space passes take
201	`ViewportManager.LayoutCamera` (exactly `Matrix.Identity` when the two spaces are
202	equal, which is why adopting it changes nothing in a single-space game). Moving a
203	game from 720p to 1080p is then a two-number diff in the head, with no coordinate
204	— and no coordinate-carrying test — recalibrated. `ViewportManager.MapMouse` is
205	the one screen→game pointer mapping; it inverts the present
206	`DestinationRectangle`, so it is robust to resize, letterboxing and the editor's
207	viewport inset for free. Details: the `rendering` premises.
208	
209	**Presentation scaling is declared, not improvised.** How the frame reaches a
210	window that is not the render resolution is a policy the game declares
211	(`ViewportManager.Policy`), resolved in one place and tried in one order:
212	**overscan** to a clean scale (the camera reveals a sliver more world, bounded by
213	a gamedev-set tolerance) → **letter/pillarbox** at a clean scale → **stretch**.
214	Whichever step wins produces the single `DestinationRectangle` that
215	`FinalDrawSystem` composites into and `MapMouse` inverts — a layer that computes
216	its own destination desyncs the pointer from the picture. Sampling is a separate,
217	per-layer question (`RenderLayer.Sampler`: `Auto` = point at an integer scale,
218	linear otherwise), resolved against that layer's own scale. The engine default is
219	`Stretch` (the historical framing); a scaffolded game declares
220	`PresentationPolicy.Default`.
221	
222	**Camera.** A `Camera` instance owns its virtual (destination) resolution and its
223	render scale (both immutable after construction) and exposes mutable zoom,
224	position, and rotation. Multiple cameras at once are explicitly supported — local
225	multiplayer or CCTV-style views. `CameraFollowSystem` is *optional*:
226	fixed-camera games or custom camera systems are valid; just don't
227	register `CameraFollowSystem` and `CullingSystem` will still read
228	whatever the `Camera` reports.
229	
230	## 5. Physics & collision
231	
232	The framework provides Newtonian-style movement, gravity, layer-based
233	collision filtering, and AABB plus convex-polygon (SAT) collision
234	detection. These pieces are independent components and systems — a
235	game can use velocity without collision, or collision without
236	gravity — and the pipeline assembler picks which to register.
237	
238	**Components.** `Velocity` carries current and last velocity vectors
239	(the delta is exposed); `RigidBody` carries mass, gravity participation,
240	kinematic flag, and freeze-axis flags. A collider is its OWN entity now
241	(colliders-as-entities): `BoxCollider` carries a centered `Size`
242	(no offset — pose comes from the collider entity's `Transform`) and
243	active layers; `ConvexCollider` carries collider-entity-local vertices,
244	world-space vertices, a broadphase AABB and active layers. `ColliderTag`
245	is auto-applied to any collider entity so detection queries can match a
246	unified tag. A collider's **body** (the entity a contact acts on) is
247	resolved via `ColliderBody.Resolve` — nearest `RigidBody`/`Velocity`
248	ancestor, else itself — and `CollisionMessage` carries both the collider
249	entities and their bodies; resolution writes corrections to the body.
250	
251	**The reference physics pipeline order**, from
252	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–286`:
253	**Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit.**
254	Each stage owns one job:
255	- *Movement* — game systems write `Velocity` based on input and AI.
256	- *Velocity (`VelocitySystem`)* — apply `Velocity` to `Transform.Position`.
257	- *Detection (`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`)* — broadphase via AABB
258	  + narrowphase via SAT for `ConvexCollider`; emit `CollisionMessage`s.
259	- *Resolution (`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` or
260	  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`)* — correct positions and
261	  velocities for contacts; honor `RigidBody` freeze flags.
262	- *Commit (`TransformCommitSystem`)* — finalize `LastPosition`, so the
263	  next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
264	
265	Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
266	reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
267	ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
268	through walls — see §3.
269	
270	**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
271	the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
272	filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
273	broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
274	that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
275	broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.
276	
277	**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
278	holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
279	thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
280	contexts.
281	
282	**Multiple colliders per body (colliders-as-entities).** A collider is its
283	own entity, so a body owns N collider children — the former
284	one-collider-of-each-type-per-entity assumption is retired. Detection
285	iterates collider entities; resolution corrects each contact's body,
286	accumulating sequentially with per-message re-validation so a body hit
287	through two of its colliders in one frame is not double-corrected. Two
288	shape components on ONE entity is still not a thing (it would be a single
289	collider entity with an ambiguous shape) — give each shape its own child
290	collider entity.
291	
292	### Aspirational direction
293	
294	Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
295	end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.
296	
297	## 6. Level loading & entity spawning
298	
299	**The shipped game boots native `.mdscene` levels only** (see "Native-only
300	load" below). The LDtk (`.ldtk`) module is now **import-only**: its loader and
301	parsers run once, off the game boot, to migrate a legacy level into a native
302	scene the game then owns. The pipeline below describes that **import** path — a
303	request loads a file, the parser walks the data, and it emits
304	`EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into entities. It is
305	composed only in the reference screen's `importMode`, never at live boot.
306	
307	**The pipeline.**
308	1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
309	2. The import composition registers **`level-ldtk`'s own
310	   `LDtkLevelLoadSystem`** as the handler for that message (in place of the
311	   native-only `LevelLoadRequestSystem` the boot path composes). It loads the
312	   LDtk file and **adds `LDtkLevelDataComponent` to the world** — the LDtk
313	   module's own level singleton, carrying the full `LDtkLevel` — plus the
314	   format-agnostic `CurrentLevelComponent(identifier)` marker and the
315	   background color.
316	3. The LDtk parsers (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`)
317	   **subscribe to `LDtkLevelDataComponent` being added** and parse on add.
318	4. Parsers emit `EntitySpawnRequest`s. Layer-derived data they can no longer
319	   pass as an LDtk type rides `CustomFields` under the `ldtk:` keys of
320	   `LDtkSpawnFields`.
321	5. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
322	   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.
323	
324	**Key invariant — `level-loading` is format-agnostic; the dependency arrow
325	points parser → plumbing.** No LDtk type appears in `level-loading` source
326	(issue #54): the shared `CurrentLevelComponent` holds a plain string
327	identifier, `EntitySpawnRequest` has no `LayerInstance` member, and
328	`LevelLoadRequestSystem` has no `ContentManager` and no format fallback.
329	Everything format-shaped lives in the format's own module — its level
330	component, its `LoadLevelRequest` handler, and its namespaced `CustomFields`
331	keys. A game that never installs `level-ldtk` therefore never compiles
332	against LDtk. When you add a format, add a module; do not add a branch or a
333	typed member to the shared plumbing.
334	
335	**Key invariant — the parsers react to component lifecycle, not
336	to push messages.** Their pattern (subscribe to their module's level
337	component being added) is the engine-wide default. A test or tool that sets
338	`LDtkLevelDataComponent` manually triggers them just as well as the regular
339	`LoadLevelRequest` path — and without a content pipeline. For new parsers,
340	follow this pattern — resist the urge to make a system "only respond when the
341	right message arrived"; that couples the system to an upstream sequence that
342	should be the assembler's choice.
343	
344	**Factory registration.** `EntitySpawnSystem` keeps a dictionary of
345	`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
346	setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
347	warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
348	throw** — this is on the backlog (§10). For now, treat the warning as a
349	high-severity signal during development.
350	
351	**Native-only load — the content-driven unification (PS5, asymmetry
352	resolved).** `LevelLoadRequestSystem` is now a **native-only** dispatcher:
353	each `LoadLevelRequest` probes for a bundled native scene
354	`Content/Levels/<id>.mdscene` via `TitleContainer` (the console-portable
355	read) and, on a hit, loads it through the generalized `SceneReaderSystem`
356	(the same native reader the editor's `LoadSceneRequest` uses —
357	reconstructing entities from serialized components, not factories). An id
358	with **no** native scene **fails loud** — there is no LDtk branch in the system
359	to fall back to (issue #54 removed it along with the `ContentManager`).
360	Native `.mdscene` is the game's real level format: versioned in
361	`Content/Levels/`, MGCB-`/copy:`-bundled, read read-only via `TitleContainer`
362	on every platform (only the desktop editor writes, PS3). **The whole LDtk module
363	is now IMPORT-ONLY machinery:** its loader + parsers run once — via the import op
364	(a headless `--export-scene <id>` / `MONODREAMS_EXPORT_SCENE` dev op, or a future
365	editor toolbar action) — to re-parse a legacy level and serialize the resulting
366	world to a native `.mdscene` the game then owns; they are **not wired to live
367	game boot** (composed only in the reference screen's `importMode`, which
368	registers `LDtkLevelLoadSystem` in place of `LevelLoadRequestSystem`). This
369	closes the parser-asymmetry backlog (§10): one content-driven load path.
370	(The Blender importer that once shared this path was retired in wave BR —
371	see §10.) Migration status: the committed
372	`Content/Levels/Blender_Level.mdscene` (a native scene originally migrated
373	from Blender) boots native; the LDtk `Level_0` is not yet migrated (its
374	~21k per-tile entities need a native tile-layer batching primitive — a
375	follow-up, §10).
376	
377	## 7. The reference pipeline
378	
379	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
380	assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
381	overall order, end-to-end:
382	
383	1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
384	   under replay.
385	2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
386	   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
387	   dialogue state).
388	3. **Physics module** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
389	   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
390	   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
391	   `TransformCommitSystem`.
392	4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
393	   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
394	5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
395	6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
396	7. **Render module** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →
397	   `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem` → `MeshPrepSystem` →
398	   `MasterRenderSystem` → debug overlays.
399	
400	Each game's screen owns its own pipeline. The reference assembly is a
401	recommendation — fixed-camera games omit `CameraFollowSystem`,
402	non-physics screens skip the physics module, UI-only screens may have
403	no game logic at all. What does not change is the *shape* of the order:
404	input first, render last, with physics ahead of hierarchy and hierarchy
405	ahead of culling.
406	
407	### Aspirational direction
408	
409	A declarative system-dependencies API would let
410	`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` say "I need `VelocitySystem` before
411	me this frame" and let the framework validate the assembly. Until that
412	exists, ordering bugs are caught by review (see the `/deep-review`
413	skill at §`.claude/skills/deep-review/SKILL.md`) and by behaviour
414	tests.

416	## 8. Debug & testing
417	
418	The engine provides a small set of debug primitives. They are
419	*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.
420	
421	**`Logger`.** A static, lock-protected singleton in
422	`MonoDreams.State.Logger`. `Initialize(outputDirectory)` must be called
423	once before use; `Shutdown()` must be called to flush. Output goes to
424	`<dir>/monodreams_<timestamp>.log` with format `[wallclock] [GT gametime]
425	[LEVEL] message`. Replaces `Console.WriteLine`. The `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`
426	environment variable redirects all debug output (logs, replay input,
427	screenshots) for test isolation.
428	
429	**Input replay.** Drop `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output
430	directory. Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type,
431	time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
432	skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
433	auto-exits when the replay finishes.
434	
435	**Pointer replay.** The input replay speaks a gamepad vocabulary and can
436	say nothing to a mouse-first screen (a menu, a business sim, a card game,
437	the editor). `debug/pointer_replay.json` — driven by the `debug` module's
438	`PointerReplaySystem` — scripts the pointer instead: `move` / `click` /
439	`wheel` / `type` / `waitUntil` / `label`, in **authoring-space**
440	coordinates, counted in **frames**. It shares the input replay's contract
441	exactly (file-gated, deterministic, fully logged, auto-exit on drain) and
442	it **injects into the real `CursorInputComponent`** rather than calling
443	handlers, so a scripted click exercises the same picking, focus and UI
444	path a hand on the mouse does. `waitUntil` is the load-bearing command:
445	without stage gating a script races the game it drives. See the `debug`
446	module's `docs/overview.md` § Pointer replay.
447	
448	**Frame capture.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` writes frames to the debug
449	directory in one of two formats: PNG (encoded off-thread; the right
450	choice for occasional verification shots, but the ~50 ms encode caps a
451	per-frame capture at ~15–26 fps) or raw RGBA (`CaptureFormat.Raw` — a
452	synchronous memcpy dump sustaining full frame rate, ~3.5 MiB per frame
453	at 1280x720). Off by default. Env-driven capture goes through
454	`ScreenshotCaptureSystem.FromEnvironment`, the single owner of the
455	`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=1|png|raw` / `MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_INTERVAL` /
456	`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_MAX_FRAMES` / `MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_TARGET`
457	contract; the replay-gated pattern (`"screenshots": true` in
458	`input_replay.json`) still drives PNG-interval capture.
459	`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_TARGET=Main|UI|HUD|Scroll|Editor` reads that
460	render target at its own fixed resolution instead of the window
461	backbuffer (default `window`), so captured evidence keeps the same
462	geometry across machines, resizes and letterboxing — the target is
463	resolved from the passes that ran, through
464	`MasterRenderSystem.RenderedTargetSink`. See the `debug` module's
465	`docs/overview.md` § Frame capture for the disk-cost table and the
466	raw-vs-encoded rationale.
467	
468	**Unattended runs.** `MONODREAMS_KEEP_AWAKE=1` makes a host hold a macOS
469	`NSProcessInfo` activity for the run (`KeepAwake.FromEnvironment`) — the
470	in-process `caffeinate -disu`. Without it, App Nap (every headless run
471	has a hidden window) or display sleep can suspend a long agentic run,
472	which shows up as a process that stops making progress rather than one
473	that fails. Opt-in, macOS-only, a logged no-op elsewhere; see the
474	`debug` module's `docs/overview.md` § Unattended runs for what the flag
475	does not cover.
476	
477	**Headless mode — two hosts, two contracts.** There are two headless
478	paths and they do *not* do the same thing:
479	
480	- **Examples** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`)
481	  creates a 1×1 off-screen window and **early-returns from `Draw`** — it
482	  runs Update-side logic at max speed but renders **nothing**. It is
483	  convenient for fast logic/replay integration tests via `GameTestRunner`
484	  but cannot observe any visual or render-path behaviour. Treat it as the
485	  logic-only path; don't rely on it for rendering correctness.
486	- **Demos** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Demos -- --headless --screen
487	  <name> --frames <N> --exit`) is the **observe-and-self-verify** path
488	  (issue #28). It keeps a real `GraphicsDevice` on a hidden, full-virtual-
489	  resolution backbuffer, **renders every frame** (`Draw` is not a no-op),
490	  dumps non-blank PNGs to `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`, logs periodic live-heap
491	  samples, and self-terminates after `<N>` frames. This is the supported
492	  way for an agent to verify its own work on the demo host without a human.
493	  See the `debug` module premises ("Headless Demos renders every frame";
494	  "Headless heap samples measure the live set") and
495	  `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`.
496	
497	A literal zero-window mode / null `GraphicsDevice` is **not** possible on
498	MonoGame DesktopGL 3.8.4 (the window hosts the GL context); a hidden
499	window that never presents is the achievable form of "headless render".
500	
501	**Testing.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` uses xUnit + the custom
502	`GameTestRunner`, which spawns the game in headless mode with a temp
503	debug directory, writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and
504	exposes log-assertion helpers (`AssertLogContains`,
505	`AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`). The gold-standard tests
506	today are `SATCollisionTests` (pure-logic), `BlenderLevelTests`
507	(native scene boot), and `InfiniteRunnerTests` (integration).
508	
509	**Test isolation is enforced, not trusted.** The whole assembly runs in
510	one process, so the engine's process-wide mutables — the sockets
511	(`Logger.LineSink`, `GatedSystem.TimingSink`,
512	`MasterRenderSystem.RenderedTargetSink`), the static switches
513	(`SystemProfiler`, the debug-overlay flags, `FinalDrawSystem`'s colours)
514	and the two singletons (`PlatformServices.Current`, the `Logger` session)
515	— are shared by every test. `MonoDreams.Tests` returns all of them to
516	their shipped defaults **after every single test**
517	(`ProcessWideStateGuardAttribute`, declared once at assembly scope) and
518	runs its classes in a **deterministic order**
519	(`DeterministicCollectionOrderer`). xUnit's default order is hash-seeded,
520	so it differs on every run: an order-dependent failure surfaces once and
521	hides for the next three, and "it passes in isolation" tells you nothing
522	(issue #114). Pinning the order makes such a failure either always there
523	or never there; `MONODREAMS_TEST_SEED=<n>` shuffles reproducibly when you
524	want to go looking, and `MONODREAMS_TEST_LAST=<substring>` forces a class
525	to run last. Add any new engine-level static to `ProcessWideState` in the
526	same PR that introduces it. See the foundation premise "A process-wide
527	socket is restored by whoever installs it — tests included".
528	
529	**No architectural tests today.** ArchUnit-style assertions
530	("`MonoDreams/Component/*.cs` must contain only data") do not exist
531	yet. Most premises in `docs/{domain}/premises.md` start their `Tests:`
532	field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.
533	
534	## 9. The editor is part of the game
535	
536	The level editor is **not a separate application** and **not a separate
537	renderer** — it is the running game under an editor run configuration.
538	There is one world, one `Camera`, and one draw stack
539	(`CullingSystem → SpritePrepSystem → YSortSystem → MeshPrepSystem →
540	TextPrepSystem → MasterRenderSystem`); the editor previews exactly what
541	the player sees because it runs that same pipeline. What changes between
542	playing and editing is not *which* pipeline runs but *which systems in
543	it are allowed to run* — a **run-state contract** the engine codifies in
544	`foundation` — and the run state is driven by a **transport**, not a
545	mode-toggle key.
546	
547	**The transport model.** Under the editor run flag (`--editor` /
548	`MONODREAMS_EDITOR=1` — the ONLY way into the editor) the shell, chrome,
549	and editor systems are **always composed and visible**; no key toggles
550	the editor away. The designer drives the game like a media player through
551	the toolbar's left-most transport buttons (or the headless
552	`Play`/`Pause`/`Restart` editor ops), owned by `EditorTransport`:
553	**Paused** = `RunMode.Edit` (game logic Freeze-gated, editing tools
554	live — the boot state under the flag), **Playing** = `RunMode.Play`
555	(the game runs inside the inset viewport; the shell stays up and the
556	transport buttons + systems panel stay interactive, but the editing
557	tools are inert — a click in the viewport belongs to the game), and
558	**Restart** = return the world to the state of the original load:
559	clear the undo history, remove the world-level **marker** components
560	(`CurrentLevelComponent` — a plain string level id now — and
561	`CurrentBackgroundColorComponent`, so the reload starts from a clean
562	world-level state; a `Set` over a still-present component fires *Changed*, not
563	*Added*. The LDtk parsers key off `level-ldtk`'s own `LDtkLevelDataComponent`,
564	which exists only in the import-op composition — where the transport never
565	runs — so it is deliberately not swept), dispose every scene entity (editor infrastructure — entities tagged
566	`EditorInfrastructureComponent` — the cursor pipeline, and
567	screen-`KeepAlive`-named infrastructure survive), re-run the screen's
568	recorded `Reload`, and land Paused. **Unsaved live edits are discarded
569	by Restart** — the standard play-mode trade-off; Save first to keep
570	them.
571	
572	**The run-state contract.** `GameState.RunMode` is one of `Play`
573	(default) or `Edit`. A system opts into run-state awareness by being
574	wrapped in a `GatedSystem` carrying an `EditTimeBehavior` policy
575	(`RunNormally` / `Freeze` / `RunPartial` / `RuntimeEditable`). Each
576	frame the gate reads `RunMode` and decides whether to forward to its
577	child: `RunNormally` runs in both modes; `Freeze` runs in `Play` only;
578	`RunPartial` and `RuntimeEditable` are reserved (today they run in both,
579	finer semantics deferred). Editor tooling is **ECS systems over this
580	gated game pipeline** — selection, gizmo, undo-apply, scene save/load,
581	and the toolbar are ordinary systems registered alongside the game's,
582	made inert while Playing by an Edit guard (the transport chrome —
583	toolbar transport buttons + systems panel — deliberately stays live in
584	both states). There is no parallel editor data model: a scene
585	round-trips by serializing the entities' components, not by re-running
586	factories.
587	
588	**Key invariant — default `Play` + opt-in gating leaves every existing
589	screen byte-identical.** `RunMode` defaults to `Play`, and only a system
590	explicitly wrapped in a `GatedSystem` changes behavior with the mode. A
591	screen that never wraps a system and never sets `Edit` behaves exactly
592	as it did before the model existed. This is what makes the run-state
593	model safe to add across all modules at once.
594	
595	**Key rule — the gating policy per system group is fixed by what editing
596	needs to see and not disturb.** Render, input, cursor, and
597	`HierarchySystem` stay live in `Edit` (`RunNormally`) — the preview must
598	keep drawing, the designer must keep clicking, and an editor's transform
599	edit must still propagate to world space the same frame. Game logic,
600	physics, collision, AI/dialogue, and `CameraFollowSystem` `Freeze` in
601	`Edit` — they would otherwise move entities out from under the designer
602	or fight the editor for the camera; in `Edit` the editor drives
603	`Camera.Position`/`Zoom` directly. Get a policy wrong and the failure is
604	silent: a frozen render module is a black screen the instant you enter
605	`Edit`; a live physics module rains gravity on entities you are trying
606	to place; a frozen `HierarchySystem` shows edits at last frame's world
607	position. The authoritative system-by-mode table is the interaction
608	matrix in the level-editor plan-contract and
609	[`docs/flows/level-editor.md`](flows/level-editor.md); the run-state
610	premises live in
611	[`MonoDreams/foundation/docs/premises.md`](../MonoDreams/foundation/docs/premises.md).
612	
613	**Editor-overlay entities are standalone.** Gizmo handles, the selection
614	highlight, and the toolbar are never `ChildOfComponent`-parented to game
615	entities, because `HierarchySystem.DisposeOrphans` runs in `Edit` and
616	would cascade-dispose them when their host entity is deleted. Deletion is
617	modeled as an undo command that snapshots the disposed sub-graph, not a
618	bare `entity.Dispose()`.
619	
620	**The editor shell is a compositing concern, not a pipeline fork.** With
621	the editor composed, the game composite renders into a smaller centered
622	viewport (`ViewportManager.SetViewportInset` — deliberately the same
623	object that inverts the mouse mapping, so picking follows for free) and
624	the editor chrome renders around it at native window resolution
625	(`RenderTargetID.Editor` + `RenderLayer.Native`). The shell is
626	**constant across transport states** — it never collapses while Playing.
627	The game pipeline itself is untouched — same passes, same targets — and
628	without the run flag nothing editor-related is constructed: zero inset,
629	no chrome layer, byte-identical to a screen without the editor. Details:
630	the `rendering` and `level-editor` premises.
631	
632	**The editor is host- and screen-agnostic, and the pipeline is
633	inspectable.** The editor does not care which host or screen is running —
634	under the editor run flag every screen of every host (a menu or a module
635	demo as much as a level) builds its pipelines through the
636	`EditorPipelineRegistrar` and composes the `EditorOverlay` over its own
637	world, declaring its own per-system edit policies at the registration
638	site (e.g. a menu freezes its button interaction in `Edit` so clicks
639	belong to the editor; a runner freezes its whole simulation block). Where
640	a screen lacks a prerequisite, the overlay supplies it (its own cursor
641	pipeline for a cursor-less screen; the `DefaultEditorKeys` key surface
642	for a host with no action mapping) or degrades gracefully (no Y-sorted
643	layer ⇒ selection picks on the final source-derived depth). The recipe
644	for wiring a new host/screen is the level-editor overview's "Adding the
645	editor to a screen/host" section. The registrar
646	is also the live inspection surface — and it owns the hierarchy: composite
647	blocks are registrar groups (`AddGroup`) with named children, built and
648	gate-wrapped by the registrar itself (DefaultEcs composites hide their
649	children, so a screen must never pre-build an opaque composite for
650	anything it wants inspectable). The editor's systems panel renders that
651	tree — every entry of both pipelines, groups indented above their
652	children, name, policy, enabled state (tri-state on groups: all/none/
653	mixed) — and toggles any of them at runtime through `SetEnabled` (leaf =
654	both-modes master switch; group = cascade over its descendant leaves), so
655	the per-system edit-mode declaration is visible and adjustable while the
656	game runs.
657	
658	**Editing produces versioned, portable, diffable levels — the persistence
659	story.** A level the editor authors is saved as a native `.mdscene` **into
660	the game's SOURCE content tree** (`Content/Levels/<id>.mdscene`), versioned
661	in git — not into the ephemeral build output. Writing is a **desktop-dev-only**
662	capability (guarded by the editor run flag + an OS check + a resolved project
663	root, resolved via `MONODREAMS_PROJECT_ROOT` or a walk-up to the `game.mdproj`
664	manifest; unresolved disables Save loudly, never crashes); **reading is
665	console-portable** — the shipped game boots a level read-only through
666	`TitleContainer` over MGCB-`/copy:`-bundled files on every platform (desktop,
667	web, consoles), native-first via `LoadLevelRequest` (§6), so straying from
668	MGCB never costs console support. The serializer is **canonical and
669	byte-stable** (deterministic bytes, stable per-entity ids ordering
670	`entities[]`), so `load → edit → save` is a fixed point and a git diff of a
671	level is meaningful. A **`game.mdproj` manifest** makes "a MonoDreams project"
672	a versionable unit (entry scene, levels dir, asset roots). A new level bundles
673	**zero-touch** — the editor appends the MGCB `/copy:` entry on first save
674	(MGCB has no glob; a build-time regen would sweep gitignored placeholder art),
675	so it boots after a normal build with no manual `.mgcb` editing. And a scene is
676	**ship-ready** (fully portable) exactly when it has **zero `file:` AssetKeys** —
677	a checkable lint (all drop-folder art graduated to MGCB content keys); the
678	committed reference levels are asserted ship-clean. The invariants live in the
679	`level-editor` and `level-loading` premises.
680	
681	**One data model — anything authored is component state on an entity,
682	singletons included; special file blocks are debt.** A scene is a set of
683	entities carrying components, and *everything the designer authors lives that
684	way* — including the singletons it is tempting to model as a special
685	top-level file block (the scene camera, and later the layer map). A `camera`
686	block, a materialized editor rig for it, bespoke edit commands, and per-mode
687	re-sync seams are **four parallel representations of one value**, and every
688	one is a place the value can silently disagree with the others. The camera is
689	the case study: three camera defects in three days (zoom edits not reaching
690	the rig or the file) all lived in that camera-only plumbing; the day the
691	camera became an ordinary `core.Camera` entity — `EntityInfoComponent("Camera")`
692	+ `TransformComponent` (one rotation, on the Transform) + `CameraComponent`
693	zoom, serialized in `entities[]` like everything else — the block, the rig,
694	the commands, and the re-sync seams all deleted, exactly as colliders stopped
695	breaking the day they became child entities (§5).
696	
697	**Corollary — Inspector-visible ⇒ Save-persisted ⇒ round-trip-owned.** If a
698	value shows up in the Inspector, Save must persist it; if Save persists it,
699	`load → save` must own it as a byte fixed point. A value that is editable but
700	not serialized (or serialized but not round-trip-stable) is a bug waiting to
701	surface as "my edit vanished on reload". The one data model is what makes this
702	hold for free: an authored value is a component, and components already
703	round-trip.
704	
705	**The extension recipe (how to add a new authored thing).** Do NOT add a file
706	block or a bespoke editor subsystem. Instead:
707	
708	1. **Define a component** with clearly named authored vs derived fields (author
709	   the source; recompute the derived — e.g. `CameraComponent.Zoom` is authored,
710	   the view matrix is derived; a collider's `Size` is authored, its world AABB
711	   derived).
712	2. **Register its serializer** (`ComponentSerializerRegistry` — engine types in
713	   `EngineComponentSerializers`, game types in the game's own registration),
714	   so it round-trips through the canonical serializer.
715	3. **Optionally add an Inspector default-initializer** so "Add ⟨component⟩"
716	   births a sane instance.
717	
718	Those three steps buy the whole authoring stack — file authoring, Inspector
719	editing, undo, dirty-tracking, prefab overrides, byte-stable diffs, and
720	Game-mode sandbox protection — **by composition, not configuration**. There is
721	no fourth step and no special case. When a value seems to *need* a file block,
722	that is the signal it wants to be a component on an entity instead. (A legacy
723	block that predates this tenet is migrated forward by the CLI umbrella
724	`monodreams migrate` — the camera block's v2→v3 lift is the reference; see the
725	`level-editor` migrator premises.)
726	
727	### Aspirational direction
728	
729	The reserved `RunPartial` / `RuntimeEditable` policies are placeholders
730	for finer edit-time behavior (a system that does reduced work, or stays
731	interactive, while editing) — they run-as-`RunNormally` today and gain
732	distinct semantics when a later wave needs them. The interaction matrix
733	is enforced by review and by the editor screen's own tests until a
734	declarative system-dependency API (§2, §7) can validate it at
735	registration time.
736	
737	## 10. Refactor backlog (named cruft)
738	
739	Carried forward from the bootstrap interview so they are not forgotten.
740	Each is either implementation debt or an aspirational direction that
741	will eventually move from "documented in CORE_TENETS" to "enforced in
742	code".
743	
744	- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
745	  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
746	  reasoning about hierarchy.
747	- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
748	  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
749	  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
750	- **`Blender_` identifier prefix / parser-asymmetry** (§6). **RESOLVED
751	  (PS5); Blender importer DELETED (wave BR).** The game boot is a single
752	  native-only dispatcher (`LevelLoadRequestSystem`): `LoadLevelRequest` →
753	  native `.mdscene` via `SceneReaderSystem`, or fail loud. The LDtk module is
754	  import-only machinery (its own `LDtkLevelLoadSystem` + parsers, composed only
755	  in the reference screen's `importMode`, run by the export op), so nothing
756	  legacy runs at boot — and since issue #54 `level-loading` carries no LDtk
757	  type at all, so the separation is structural, not a flag. The
758	  Blender importer that once shared the `Blender_` name-prefix dispatch was
759	  retired wholesale in wave BR (parser + data types + exporter plugin + CLI
760	  registry entry + module-count docs), so the name-prefix hack is gone
761	  end-to-end — no parser asymmetry remains. Residual: the LDtk `Level_0` is
762	  not yet migrated to native (it needs a **native tile-layer batching
763	  primitive** — a compact representation for ~21k per-tile entities, so its
764	  `.mdscene` isn't a multi-MB per-entity dump); until then it is import-only
765	  and not offered by the reference menu. When the LDtk parser too is
766	  eventually deleted, the import op moves to a standalone tool.
767	- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
768	  Intended behaviour is to throw.
769	- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
770	  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
771	  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
772	- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
773	  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
774	  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
775	  contract.
776	- **Folder layout** (`Component/<subdomain>/` vs `Component/<file>/`
777	  inconsistency). Intended end-state is **modular packs** (Spring Data
778	  / Spring Security analog) — `MonoDreams.Rendering`,
779	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
780	- **Examples headless mode is logic-only** (§8). Its `Draw` early-returns,
781	  so it renders nothing — fine for replay/logic tests, useless for visual
782	  observation. The Demos headless path (issue #28) is the load-bearing
783	  observe-and-self-verify route and *does* render; the remaining debt is
784	  that the Examples mode is still named "headless" despite not rendering,
785	  and the two paths could eventually share one host abstraction.
786	- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
787	  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today. The
788	  one exception is the **manifest-honesty check** (issue #83,
789	  `MonoDreams.Cli.Tests/ManifestHonestyTests.cs`): every module is
790	  scaffolded, `add`ed and built against its *declared* dependencies alone,
791	  in CI, per module.
792	- **Module manifests that under-declare** (§1, tooling). Surfaced by the
793	  manifest-honesty check and listed there as known gaps — each one is a
794	  project that does not compile after `monodreams add <module>`:
795	  `ui` and `level-editor` omit modules they import (`cursor`, `camera`
796	  respectively — both acyclic, one-line manifest fixes); `dialogue` omits
797	  both `cursor` and the `MonoGame.Framework.Content.Pipeline` package its
798	  YarnSpinner importer needs; `foundation` (`ScreenController` takes
799	  `rendering`'s `ViewportManager`/`Camera`) and `rendering`
800	  (`DrawComponent`/`MasterRenderSystem` read `rendering-text`'s
801	  `DynamicTextComponent.DefaultLineSpacing`) cannot declare their way out —
802	  both would be cycles, so the coupling has to move in code. Until
803	  `foundation` + `rendering` are fixed, the check installs a compile floor
804	  and every scaffolded game inherits the same two modules whether it wants
805	  them or not.
806	- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
807	  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
808	  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.
809	- **Test or example per public contract** (§2). Several messages
810	  (`PositionChangeMessage`, `SizeChangeMessage`, `RigidBodyTouchMessage`)
811	  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
812	  contract should ship with at least one usage.
